title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with a synthetic likeness. A caller on a WhatsApp video call presented himself as a sitting Chief Minister, in both appearance and voice, and used that borrowed identity to make an offer of financial aid. The deepfake was not the product of a company deploying a system, it was a tool used directly against one person, and the only check on the caller's identity was the victim's own eyes and ears on a consumer video call.

The failure sits at the point of contact, where the visual and audio channel is the sole evidence of who is speaking. Nothing in that channel verifies identity, and nothing between the call and the payment app verified it either. Catching this would have required confirming the caller and the aid scheme through an official channel independent of the call itself, and treating a request for advance fees as the signal it is. The later demand, made by someone claiming to be a CBI officer, rested on the same unverified claim of authority.

What is not established is who made the calls, whether the person who appeared on the video produced the deepfake, or whether the claimed CBI involvement was anything other than a claim. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act, which is a step in an investigation and not a finding against anyone.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, lost more than Rs 1.04 lakh after a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9. The caller used an AI deepfake to look and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and actor C Joseph Vijay. The fake Vijay offered Rs 11 lakh in financial aid and said a manager would arrange a transfer from a foreign account in dollars. The manager first asked for Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, then Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN.

Later, someone claiming to be Thakur from the CBI demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid through a digital payment app, totaling over Rs 1.04 lakh. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been cheated. He called the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then went to Byappanahalli police. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act. Police warned people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them.
